items.syntax: SELECT … FROM a JOIN b ON b.key = a.key
items.explanation: Returns pairs that match; rows without a partner disappear.
items.example: SELECT o.order_id, c.company_name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id LIMIT 5;

items.syntax: SELECT … FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.key = a.key
items.explanation: Rows from a without a match get NULLs for b's columns.
items.example: SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id ORDER BY o.order_id NULLS FIRST LIMIT 5;
items.expected: Customers with their orders; FISSA and PARIS first with NULL order_id.

items.syntax: LEFT JOIN b ON … WHERE b.key IS NULL
items.explanation: Anti-join: keeps left rows that found no partner.
items.example: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_details od ON od.product_id = p.product_id WHERE od.product_id IS NULL;

items.syntax: FROM a RIGHT JOIN b ON …
items.explanation: Mirror of LEFT JOIN; usually rewritten as LEFT JOIN with tables swapped.
items.example: SELECT o.order_id, e.first_name FROM orders o RIGHT JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = o.employee_id LIMIT 5;

items.syntax: FROM a FULL JOIN b ON …
items.explanation: Matched pairs plus unmatched rows from each side, padded with NULLs.
items.example: SELECT e.employee_id, o.order_id FROM employees e FULL JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.employee_id WHERE e.employee_id IS NULL OR o.order_id IS NULL;
items.expected: The order with no employee (and any employee with no orders).

items.explanation: Cartesian product: rows(a) × rows(b). No ON clause.
items.example: SELECT s.company_name AS shipper, c.category_name FROM shippers s CROSS JOIN categories c LIMIT 6;

items.syntax: FROM t a JOIN t b ON b.parent = a.id
items.explanation: Two aliases give the table two roles, e.g. employee and manager.
items.example: SELECT e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = e.reports_to;
items.expected: Each employee with their manager's first name.

items.syntax: FROM a JOIN b ON … JOIN c ON …
items.explanation: Each JOIN adds one table; follow foreign keys step by step.
items.example: SELECT c.category_name, p.product_name, od.quantity FROM order_details od JOIN products p ON p.product_id = od.product_id JOIN categories c ON c.category_id = p.category_id LIMIT 5;
items.expected: 5 order lines with product and category names.

items.explanation: USING merges the key into one output column.
items.example: SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name FROM order_details JOIN products USING (product_id) LIMIT 5;

items.syntax: LEFT JOIN b ON b.key = a.key AND b.col = x
items.explanation: Conditions on the right table belong in ON; in WHERE they turn the LEFT JOIN into an inner join.
items.example: SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS heavy_orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.freight > 100 GROUP BY c.customer_id ORDER BY heavy_orders LIMIT 5;
items.expected: Customers with their count of high-freight orders, zeros included.
